public_rationale: In The Verge’s April 2, 2026 interview, Suleyman said superintelligence was “really about” whether models could deliver product value for millions of enterprises [e1]. This presents enterprise value as the central criterion without stating a requirement to exceed the smartest humans, supporting the claim about his public framing [e1].
limitations: The published interview does not establish a formal change to Microsoft’s technical definition [e1].
The April framing does not establish that Suleyman abandoned the beyond-human capabilities envisaged in his earlier essay [e1, e2].

our_interpretation: The claim concerns Suleyman’s public framing in early April 2026.
The ordinary reading of 'tried to redefine' includes presenting enterprise usefulness as what superintelligence means. It does not require a formal change to Microsoft’s technical definitions.
Describing enterprise usefulness only as an application, while expressly retaining the superhuman-capability requirement, would not establish the claimed redefinition.
criteria.support_condition: An attributable statement presents enterprise product value as the meaning or central criterion of superintelligence, without requiring performance beyond the smartest humans.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The original statement expressly preserves the superhuman-capability requirement and presents enterprise value only as a separate application or business objective.

evidence.locator: Body paragraph beginning 'Superintelligence — along with AGI'
evidence.explanation: The original interview immediately attributes to Suleyman an explanation of superintelligence in terms of models supplying enterprise product value. This supports Marcus’s reading as public reframing, although it does not establish a formal technical change.
Suleyman’s earlier account explicitly envisaged capabilities beyond humans. This cautions against treating the April business framing as proof that he abandoned that broader conception.
